title: const with Pointers
html:
const can protect the pointed-to data, the pointer itself, or both. Read the declaration right to left.

DeclarationRead asChange *p?Change p?
int *ppointer to intYesYes
const int *p (= int const *p)pointer to const intNoYes
int *const pconst pointer to intYesNo
const int *const pconst pointer to const intNoNo

const in function parameters

Key point

Converting T * → const T * is implicit and safe. The reverse (const T * → T *) needs a cast, and writing through the result to a truly const object is undefined behaviour.

Do

Mark every pointer parameter you only read as const — size_t strlen(const char *s), void print(const struct item *it).

Avoid

Cast const away to “make it compile”.

What is the difference between const char *p, char const *p and char *const p?

The first two are identical: a (modifiable) pointer to read-only chars. The third is a read-only pointer to modifiable chars — p must be initialised and can never point elsewhere. Rule: const applies to what is on its left, or to the right if nothing is on the left.

Can a const variable be modified through a pointer?

Only by casting away const, and if the object was defined const the result is undefined behaviour (it may live in read-only memory, or the compiler may have folded its value into the code).
